title: Sometimes a Key Fact Alters the Decision
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece argues that a single critical fact can overturn a leader's whole view of a decision. It gives everyday examples, such as a natural disaster before a trip or a contract clause before signing, to show how such a fact changes assumptions, risks or priorities. The author ties this to Inverse Analysis, which works backward from a desired outcome and so tends to surface hidden facts. The move is to recast good decision-making as an active hunt for the one fact not yet uncovered, pursued even though leaders half hope not to find it. It closes on the claim that every bad decision traces back to something the decision-maker did not know.
points: One critical fact can invalidate prior assumptions, reveal hidden risks or shift priorities, changing the decision entirely.
You recognize a critical fact because your perspective shifts instantly, without much discussion.
Inverse Analysis, working backward from the desired outcome, is largely a method for finding critical facts.
Good leaders presume an undiscovered fact exists and hunt for it, even while hoping not to find one.
Every bad decision, in retrospect, rests on something the decision-maker did not know.
quotes: On occasion, one fact changes everything about how a leader views an opportunity or problem. This critical fact completely alters the context, understanding, or implication of a given decision. As a result of this critical fact, leaders make a different choice.

We know we have uncovered a critical fact when upon learning it, our perspective instantly shifts. Without much discussion or thought, we know immediately that this critical fact has invalidated our previous assumptions, revealed hidden or unknown risks, or shifted our priority.
By working backward from a desired outcome and determining the steps or conditions necessary to achieve it, critical facts often emerge that couldn’t be seen in the normal decision-making process.

In their desire to make a quality decision, good leaders presume there is one fact, yet uncovered, that will change everything about their thinking. They constantly hunt for just such a fact with the secret hope that they don’t find one.

What critical fact are you missing? In retrospect, every bad decision is a direct result of something the decision-maker didn’t know. Good leaders do their very best to uncover the critical fact that will change their thinking.
